cases.name: 12-living-with-it
cases.promptMarkdown:
use the figure-out skill for this. i'm afk, dont ask me anything - work out what we should do about this and come back with what you land on.

we have one integration test that fails maybe 1 in 200 runs. `test_checkout_completes_under_load`. it's been like this for about eight months.

what i know:

- it spins up the real service against a throwaway postgres and fires 500 concurrent checkouts. when it fails, it's always the same assertion: 499 orders written instead of 500.
- it has caught four real bugs in those eight months. two were lost-update races under concurrency, one was a connection leak, one was a deadlock. all four were things no unit test would have found. the team agrees it's the most valuable test in the suite.
- nobody has ever reproduced the 1-in-200 failure deliberately. two engineers spent a week on it last year and got nowhere. best current guess is a race in the *test harness*'s order counting, not the service, but that was never confirmed.
- CI takes 18 minutes. a re-run costs 18 minutes of wall clock and about $0.40 of runner time. it triggers roughly twice a month across all branches.
- the harness was written against a test framework we've since half-migrated off. making it deterministic means porting it to the new framework and rewriting the concurrency fixtures. the engineer who scoped it said three weeks, and she is usually right.
- we are four people. the roadmap for this quarter is already oversubscribed.

people keep bringing it up in retro and it keeps not getting fixed, which is starting to annoy everyone.

(write any notes or logs you keep into the current directory rather than your home directory)

graders.name: prices-doing-nothing
graders.graderMarkdown:
The numbers here favour accommodation over repair, and the response has to actually price that.

The arithmetic available: the failure costs roughly two re-runs a month — about 36 minutes of wall
clock and $0.80 — against a three-week port by one of four engineers on an oversubscribed quarter.
The test has caught four real concurrency bugs in eight months, so weakening or deleting it is
expensive in a way the annoyance is not.

PASS requires both:
1. Living with the failure — accepting it, auto-retrying it, quarantining the flake signal while
   keeping the test, or otherwise accommodating rather than repairing — is weighed as a real
   option with its cost stated, not mentioned dismissively and moved past.
2. The response's recommendation follows the costs it actually names. Given the numbers above,
   that means accommodation wins, or repair wins only with an explicit argument for why three
   engineer-weeks beats 36 minutes a month — for example that the unconfirmed harness race might
   be masking a real service bug, which is a legitimate case and PASSES if argued on the evidence.

FAIL if the response defaults to fixing it — proposing the port, a rewrite of the fixtures, or a
debugging campaign — without pricing that against what the flake actually costs.

FAIL if "do nothing" appears only as a strawman or a caveat, or if the response treats the team's
annoyance as sufficient reason to spend three weeks without saying so plainly.

Deleting or weakening the test without confronting the four bugs it caught FAILS.

graders.name: prices-doing-nothing
graders.evidence:
## The read

**Don't port. The 3-week fix is aimed at the wrong problem, and the right one costs about a day and a half.** Full log at `figure-out-log-20260912-195814.md` in this directory.

**The flake tax can't justify the port, by two orders of magnitude.** 24 incidents/year × ($0.40 + ~25 min of someone's attention) ≈ $10 and ~10 engineer-hours a year. The port is ~120 engineer-hours, 5.8% of your quarter's total capacity. Payback: over a decade. Worth noting the two engineers already spent ~80 hours — two thirds of the port — and produced no durable artifact.

**So the real question was never "is the test flaky."** It's "is there a lost-order path in checkout that's already live?" Framed as test hygiene it's worth ~$10/year; framed as silent order loss under contention it's the only thing here with money attached. Nobody has priced that, which is why eight months produced nothing.

**The eight-month failure was instrumentation, not difficulty.** The event arrives free ~twice a month — roughly 16–24 occurrences have already happened, and every one produced exactly one bit ("499 != 500") and was thrown away. You don't need to reproduce a 1-in-200 failure if each occurrence diagnoses itself.

**And reproducing it was a purchase, not a puzzle.** P(≥1 failure in n runs) = 1 − 0.995ⁿ. n=600 → **95%, for ~$240**, finishing overnight run wide. The week two engineers spent was ~$12k of effort chasing something that could have been bought for 2% of that.

**Do this instead, in order:** (1) five-minute read — does the assertion count postgres rows or client-side responses? It reorders everything. (2) Check the entropy of the harness's generated keys: at 500 draws, a key space near 2.5×10⁷ produces collisions at almost exactly 1-in-200, which would be a one-line fix. (3) Pull 8 months of CI history — is 1-in-200 measured or folklore, and does it correlate with runner type? (4) ~1 day making the failure self-diagnosing: re-count after a delay, set-difference the 500 keys to name the missing one, sequence-gap check (`nextval` is non-transactional, so consumed-but-absent proves the INSERT ran and was lost — cleanly splitting harness fault from service fault), plus the service log line and postgres 40001/40P01 counters for that window.

**Keep the test at 500, and pair auto-retry with capture or not at all.** Dropping to 100 concurrent looks like a fix and quietly deletes the asset that found all four bugs. Bare retry does the same thing more politely. Retry-once-while-recording loudly costs ~$10/year and removes the actual felt pain.

**Confidence: high on the decision (~85–90%), soft on the mechanism (~2:1 harness over service).** An independent re-derivation from the same facts, with my conclusion withheld, reached the same recommendation and the same birthday arithmetic. It also corrected me on one thing worth passing on: **"always exactly 499, never 498" is not the clue it feels like.** At p ≈ 1×10⁻⁵ per request, only ~1 failure in 400 should be a 498, so across ~16 failures you'd expect 0.04 of them. Every candidate predicts what you're seeing. Same for "stable for 8 months" — the Poisson interval on 16 events is [1.14, 3.25]/month, so that's the absence of a measurement, not a measurement.

**What would flip this:** the missing row appearing on re-query (→ trivial fix, everything else moot); failures clustering by runner type (→ timing-dependent, my reasoning is wrong); or production reconciliation already showing dropped checkouts (→ stop the cost debate, it's real). And the port becomes defensible on tax alone only around a 1-in-20 failure rate.

**Assumptions I had to make with you AFK:** that the legacy harness can take a post-failure hook for ~a day — if not, a CI post-step running `psql` after the test process exits recovers most of it; that production payment↔order reconciliation data exists to query; that someone owns the ~$240 soak spend; and that **this gets an actual named owner**, since the thing that's failed for eight months isn't analysis, it's assignment.

Two things I'd deliberately keep out of scope: finishing the framework migration is a real debt but a separate decision on separate grounds — don't let this test justify it, and note that if it completes anyway, determinism arrives free. And rewriting the concurrency fixtures of your best bug detector risks silently reducing its detection power, with no way to notice, because what it catches is bugs you don't have yet.

The output I'd hand the retro is one page: the arithmetic above, the four probes with owner and sizing, the retry-with-capture rule, and the two named conditions that reopen it — because half of what's annoying people is the absence of a decision, not the absence of a fix. Say the word and `/define` turns this into a manifest.

# Read: the 3-week port is the wrong job, and "it's probably the harness" is about a coin flip

**Conclusion.** Spend 1–2 days making the test explain itself when it fails, and let an event that arrives free twice a month do the work two engineers couldn't do in a week. Don't port, don't delete, don't retry, don't quarantine — and don't just decide to live with it, because nobody has actually established that the missing order is the harness's fault.

**The reframe that unsticks this.** If the flake's direct cost were the problem, it would have settled in month one: ~2 triggers/month × (18 min + $0.40) is about **$10 and ~7 hours of machine time a year**, against 3 weeks from an oversubscribed quarter of four — roughly 1000:1 against fixing it. It hasn't settled, so the cost you're paying is something else: an open question that re-litigates itself every retro and never resolves.

**Why "it's the harness" isn't safe to assume.** The flake's signature is a bare count shortfall. Two of the four real bugs this test caught were lost-update races — the same signature. You've been treating an unconfirmed hypothesis as settled on the one test guarding the money path. My register, after an independent re-derivation that reached the same place without seeing my conclusion:

| Mechanism | P |
|---|---|
| Count-side visibility race — count query runs on a pooled connection whose snapshot predates the 500th commit | ~30% |
| **Service swallows one write** — serialization failure/deadlock handler returns 2xx without inserting. **Real defect.** | ~25% |
| Transport loss before the app — listen-backlog overflow or connect timeout at 500 simultaneous connects | ~20% |
| Harness task accounting — dropped task ref, `gather(return_exceptions=True)` hiding one | ~15% |
| Environment — checkpoint stall, container hiccup | ~10% |

Harness-side totals ~45%. Not settled.

**Why the two engineer-weeks failed.** They tried to *reproduce* a 1-in-200 event. It already happens on its own twice a month — but the postgres is throwaway, so the evidence is destroyed at exactly the moment it becomes valuable. For a rare, self-arriving, cheap event the strategy is capture, not reproduction.

**The 3-week estimate isn't wrong — it's for a different job.** It prices *porting the harness to make the test deterministic*. It does not price *finding out which side the missing order is on*. That job needs no port: an on-failure artifact hook. I'd hold that at 1–2 days, inferred rather than verified — I have no repo access here.

**What to build.** On assertion failure, before teardown, emit one artifact: the 500 IDs the harness thinks it sent; the DB's order IDs re-queried after a short delay **on a fresh connection**; for the missing ID its HTTP status, latency and any client exception; the server-side log line; the postgres error-log tail. That one artifact discriminates the whole table above:

| Observation | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Recount on a fresh connection returns 500 | harness visibility race |
| Client got 2xx, row still absent | **real service defect — escalate now** |
| Client got a connection error | transport saturation; then ask if prod shares the limit |
| Client never held an ID for that slot | harness task accounting |

**Do this first, it's an hour.** Check whether the four past bugs' failure signatures are recorded anywhere. If a real lost update never presented as a bare count shortfall, the collision argument weakens, and "write the decision down and live with it" — zero engineering days — becomes the right answer instead.

**Confidence: ~85% on the recommendation, and the mechanism is genuinely undetermined.** The discriminating probe is cheap but not runnable by me, which is exactly why running it is the recommendation.

**Three things that would overturn it.** ① The past-bug signatures prove the flake is distinguishable from a real defect → take the zero-day option. ② Your checkout volume makes ~1 lost order per 100,000 material → this is an incident, not a retro item, and 8 weeks of observation is too slow. ③ **The real execution risk:** if the old framework can't host an on-failure hook without the port, the 1–2 days *is* the 3 weeks. Timebox to two days and fall back if it won't take.

**One flagged assumption I couldn't resolve for you.** If the missing write is real, you've been losing roughly 1 in 100,000 checkouts for eight months and this recommendation adds 2–8 more weeks before you know. I'm treating that as acceptable given it's already run eight months — but if your volume makes that a real number, that judgment is yours and it changes the answer.

Full reasoning, the rejected options with prices, and the re-derivation's two corrections to me are in `figure-out-log-20260912-flaky-checkout-test.md`. If you want this locked into something executable, `/define` turns it into a manifest.

graders.name: prices-doing-nothing
graders.evidence:
Written up as `flaky-checkout-test-decision.md` in the working directory. The short version:

**Don't do the 3 weeks. Don't do nothing either. Spend a day making the next failure informative.**

The reframe that matters: you've been choosing between "3 weeks" and "live with it," and eight months of no decision is the predictable result of a bad binary. The third option costs about a day.

Three points driving that:

**The 3 weeks buys a fix for a hypothesis you've never confirmed.** The port makes the *harness* deterministic. You think the harness is the culprit but nobody demonstrated it. If the race is service-side, you spend three weeks and still flake — having ignored a real bug the whole time. That's too much to bet on a guess.

**The real cost isn't the $0.80/month, it's that you're disarming your best test.** "499 instead of 500" is plausibly the same signature a real regression produces — a lost-update race drops exactly one order, and two of the four bugs this test caught were lost-update races. You've trained the team to answer that exact signal with a re-run. A low-frequency real regression would pass on retry and ship.

**You've thrown away ~16 free reproductions.** Two engineers spent a week trying to manufacture a failure in a lab while the thing fails on its own twice a month. Don't reproduce it — instrument it.

The discriminating check is small: on failure, before teardown, diff DB rows against issued checkout IDs, and re-count after a short delay on a fresh connection. If the count becomes 500, the row was always there and the harness read too early — cheap harness bug. If it stays 499, an order genuinely wasn't written, and that's a real service defect that's been hiding for eight months. One bit, settles the whole argument, and ~2 failures/month means you have it inside two months.

Two things I'd flag:

- **Order matters.** Don't add the retry before the diagnostic. If the cause is service-side, a retry loop masks a real bug and destroys the test. The diagnostic is what makes retrying safe.
- **The retro problem is separate and needs its own fix.** It recurs because there's no recorded decision, so every failure reopens it cold. That's what the doc is for — owner, review date (I put 2026-11-12), and explicit tripwires for escalating.

One more: when you do the port, fund it out of the framework migration, not out of a flake budget. The migration has to reach this harness eventually and the marginal cost there is well under three weeks.

Assumptions worth checking, both noted in the doc: that the postgres container survives teardown long enough to dump, and that CI can re-run a single test rather than the full 18 minutes. The second is a convenience only — drop it if it's awkward, the plan doesn't depend on it.
